The Constitution

The second motive is to have our Constitutionmaking become a source of agreement and pride in the country rather than a source of conflict and anger. The great irony is that the government is using a constitutional process which drives Canadians apart at the very time when, in other aspects of our lives, Canadians are coming together.
Over the last decade in particular there have been great and positive changes in two regions in this country, Quebec and western Canada, changes most of all in self-confidence. In both those regions, people feel equal to Canadians from other regions. They want to play a major role in building a great country. This feeling is there but it has not always been there.
1 can remember times, growing up in western Canada, when the sense of having to suffer some kind of inequality was simply something to be borne. There was the sense that western Canadians could compete as equals. I am sure that if Quebecers spoke from their hearts in this House, they would tell us there have been times when their sense of subordination to the English was profound. Well, that sense is not now in Quebec, nor is it in western Canada. What is there instead is a sense of pride and confidence and a determination to get on with building a great country.
The tragic irony is that at a time when there was that sense of Canadians wanting to build together and when regions which had felt inferior began to feel equal, instead of using that great emotion and that great sense of Canada to build common Canadian purposes, this government brought in a measure which drives Canadians apart. Our Constitution could be a source of Canadian pride and unity. Our Constitution has been made a source of Canadian shame and division. That is the result to which we object most absolutely here, and it is for that reason that we intend to use every device which is available to us to change public opinion, to change this resolution, and to stop this government from bringing through a constitutional package that would be bad and divisive for our country.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, the constitutional resolution before us is simple and compelling. It will give us our own Constitution with an amending formula and with a charter of fundamental rights and freedoms. It recognizes the rights of Canada's Indian, Inuit and Metis peoples. It ensures that children may be educated, where numbers warrant, in either of our two official languages. It recognizes the rich heritage that people from so many different ethnic backgrounds and cultures have brought to Canada. It enshrines the principle of equalization, recognizing that in sharing our immeasurable resources and in working together to meet new and unforeseen challenges we will continue to be one of the most fortunate nations in the world.
Last May, during the vote on separation, all parties in this House and all provincial premiers made a commitment to constitutional reform and to renewed federalism. We are now honouring that commitment. Our commitment and our Constitution will enable us to get on with the task of building, through negotiation, a new and better way of sharing powers and responsibilities with the provinces. This is the base on which we will build a modern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised when I listened to the speech of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). He stated that the Progressive Conservative Party was the only one to support Quebec's position on the constitutional issue. I would like to ask him a few questions. Can he explain to Quebecers what the Vancouver formula will do to help Quebec share its basic rights as a province, which rights differ from those of the other provinces? I would also like to ask him what this government has done in support of the linguistic rights of Quebecers.
I suggest that we have done a great deal to demonstrate that Quebec is important for Canada, and I would like to tell the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that when he speaks of the divisions which have been created in this country, I have not seen any at this time, but he can expect the greatest division not to be in our country. This division will be among those who are blind. Most Canadians, or at least 85 per cent of the population, support the entrenchment of a charter of basic rights in our own Canadian Constitution.

I should like to say that at the heart of the resolution before us is the relationship it seeks to establish between individuals and the state. The state will not be able to deny fundamental freedoms such as freedom of speech or freedom to worship in one's own religion. Governments will not be able to erect barriers against Canadians moving freely from coast to coast or seeking work in any province. Every individual will be protected against discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or physical disability. And finally, the Constitution guarantees important legal rights. I wish to focus my comments on some of these legal rights, Mr. Speaker, and on why they must be entrenched.
I speak of security against unreasonable search and seizure; the right on being arrested to retain counsel and as well to be informed of the right to have counsel; the right to habeas corpus; to trial within a reasonable time; to reasonable bail; to trial by jury for serious offences; protection against cruel and unusual punishment and, most important, specific remedies are made available where any such legal rights or any of the rights or freedoms guaranteed in the charter have been infringed or denied.
If there were to be an improper search or seizure, for example, the official involved could be subject to a fine or perhaps even to suspension. If excessive force were used, the victim could be awarded damages by a court. If a municipality were to deny a religious group a licence for a gathering, a court could overrule that and order, by mandamus, that a permit be issued. It could award damages. If a school board
February 23, 1981

were to deny second language education, it could be compelled to supply it if numbers warrant.
An important right and one which I think demonstrates the essence of what we are achieving in terms of human rights is provided in the case where evidence is obtained illegally. The constitutional resolution amends our present law. It states that where constitutional rights have been broken in gathering evidence, the court can grant a number of remedies, including such evidence being declared inadmissible. This will occur only in circumstances where the court can determine that its admission would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. [Translation]
That is one way the charter could balance the protection of the individual against arbitrary or excessive use of government authority and the protection of society against crime. We have not adopted the American rule which prohibits the production of evidence, however relevant, as proof of guilt if such evidence is obtained illegally. If such a rule were implemented in Canada it would generate a feeling of frustration among law enforcement officers and also among citizens since the rule itself or a simple violation of the rules could lead automatically to acquittal.
The charter would seem to improve upon the existing legislation which, in most cases, allows the production of illegally obtained evidence. Therefore, this new provision strikes a balance between the individual's rights and the collective need for an effective enforcement of the law and for an equitable judicial system. Consequently, a piece of evidence which is considered relevant, even though it may have been obtained illegally, will be allowed unless its production might bring discredit upon the administration of justice.

Our courts, under the legal rights provision, will be able to decide, for example, whether a search was conducted in a reasonable manner. They will be able to determine whether it was reasonable that a 15-year-old girl who was arrested for jaywalking, or a pregnant woman who was arrested for not having paid a speeding ticket, should be subjected to the humiliation of a strip search. They will be able to determine whether, in the case of raids, the police have acted within reasonable strengths and within reasonable bounds or whether activities now under study by the McDonald Royal Commission were reasonable in the circumstances. If the court should determine that they were not, then the victims will have a remedy available to them.
The charter entrenches another most important right, namely, a person's right not only to obtain and instruct counsel but also to be informed of the right to have counsel. This is a progressive step which recognizes that rights should not only be available but they must be made known.
Another such right which I am proud to see in this constitution is that trials must be held within a reasonable time. Every individual who is accused and arrested should have the oppor-
The Constitution
tunity to have his or her guilt or innocence determined quickly. This is not only fair but, when you consider that it costs about $30,000 a year to keep a person in detention, it also makes good economic sense.
Some have said that we need not entrench these and other basic legal rights in a constitution, that it is sufficient for us to leave them to our federal and provincial law makers and to the common law. Let us, therefore, examine this proposition together. First, we do have a Bill of Rights that mentions some, but not all, of the rights contained in the constitutional resolution. How strong are these rights and how good a job do they do? Look at the Lavell case. Mrs. Lavell, an Indian, married a non-Indian. Under the Indian Act, she lost her status rights even though the same would not have happened had she been a man. At that time the Bill of Rights precluded discrimination based on sex. The Supreme Court held that it could not overrule the Indian Act; it was just another act along with the Bill of Rights. In similar circumstances, Sandra Lovelace has had to appeal to the United Nations because no appeal was available in Canada. When freedom from discrimination based on sex, or on any other ground, is set down in our Constitution, it will take precedence over every other law, federal, provincial or municipal. That is why we need entrenchment.
Second, we need entrenchment because even the long and prestigious history of the common law of Great Britain has indicated that it may not, in itself, prove capable of protecting important freedoms. For example, last October 21,000 U.K. prison guards went on strike. They were not available to escort accused persons to court hearings under habeas corpus. The response of the Home Secretary was to introduce a bill in Parliament authorizing the suspension of habeas corpus. So much for rights which are not entrenched in a Constitution.
Third, it is true, as many members opposite have said, that Canada is enriched by its diversity. We respect that diversity. We respect the diversity of its peoples, its geography, its customs and its traditions. The fact that we respect this diversity and are enriched by it does not mean our basic minimum rights and freedoms should be diverse, different and disparate. On the contrary, is it not fair and just that Canadians from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island, from our southern border to our far north, should enjoy the same basic minimum human rights? There should be no second-class citizens. Provinces should not have the right, as hon. members of the opposition advocate, to opt out of guaranteeing basic, minimum human rights.
Hear, hear!

Let me cite some facts which illustrate the nature of this problem. At present, we have 11 different bills of rights in Canada, one federal and ten provincial. Seven provinces provide no protection for the physically handicapped. No province protects the mentally disabled. Three provinces provide no or only limited rights for women. Five provinces do not protect the aged in their charters. Furthermore, it is desirable that basic legal rights, such as the right to a speedy

trial and reasonable bail, should be available, not only for federal criminal offences but for the numerous provincial offences, such as highway traffic, liquor and environmental laws.
A major argument against entrenchment is that it will leave questions of interpretation, and thus the application of rights and freedoms in specific cases, to the determination of our courts. Some say this will deny the supremacy of Parliament. To this argument, our only response can be: "So be it." The courts now determine which of our powers are federal and which are provincial. Every day, the courts are called upon to dispense justice and to interpret the rights of individuals. It is merely a logical progression to give them additional authority to interpret our fundamental rights and freedoms as individuals.
1 would rather see the courts charged with this responsibility than leave a free hand to legislators, legislators who have in the past shown themselves capable of enacting laws which disenfranchised Chinese Canadians, which abolished the use of French in Manitoba, which denationalized the citizenship of Japanese Canadians, which suppressed freedom of religion and speech in provinces, which restrained public assemblies and which limited the use of English in the province of Quebec. Life has changed considerably since the nineteenth century when doctrines such as Parliamentary supremacy were adumbrated. We no longer fear the power of a monarch. What does concern us is the incredible multiplicity of regulations, rules, orders and directives that are not debated in Parliament and which can infringe basic rights. These regulations emanate from the numerous bureaucracies and regulatory agencies created at the federal level, the ten provincial levels and at thousands of municipal levels.
Hear, hear!

While the task force on regulatory reform made many recommendations that would open up the regulatory process to public scrutiny and to accountability of legislators, we believe entrenching the fundamental rights contained in this constitution bill will help to avoid abuses of the rights of individuals when they arise.
In 1976, with the agreement of all provinces, Canada ratified the universal declaration that has now become the international bill of rights. In both drafting and amending our charter, the international bill served as a touchstone. It would bother me were we not prepared to take every step here in Canada to implement, foster and protect those rights which we have agreed to by international treaty.
To summarize, entrenching a charter is a declaration to Canadians and others that we believe first in protecting human rights and freedoms. We believe these rights and freedoms should not be brushed aside by a transient majority in any legislative body.
I wish to quote the words of a former prime minister, Lester B. Pearson, who said:
In short, freedom and welfare must be kept in a healthy balance or there will be trouble. This essential balance can be achieved by applying, to every proposal for further intervention by the state, the question: will it truly benefit the individual; will it enlarge or restrict his opportunity for self-expression and development?
Governments are elected to serve the needs of all people, not their own. Their highest calling is to protect individual rights and freedoms. Those who would deny Canadians this Constitution that we propose because we have not obtained the unanimous support of the provinces are closing their eyes to the present and turning their backs on the future.
Why haven't they supported it?

The hon. members asks why the provinces have not supported this resolution. I am happy to trace the course of history in recent times. We have seen one province seeking to bargain rights for higher oil prices, one province seeking to bargain rights for offshore oil resources. We see one province whose leader is dedicated to separation and is committed to ensuring that federalism in Canada does not work.
We are not using the wrong process to break a deadlock. We are using the only process to obtain our own Constitution with an entrenched charter of rights, something which is sought by 85 per cent of the Canadian people. We are at a crossroads and it is time to act. History will record this measure as an act of statesmanship and national building of the highest order. I am proud to support it.
Mr. Speaker, I know the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is going to leave now because he does not want to hear the blame he is going to receive from me.
He does not want to hear the truth.

He never wants to hear the truth. That is why he is not going to the people on the Constitution.
1 have followed this debate with great interest over the past weeks and, indeed, months. There have been some good speeches, some emotional speeches. The last speech by the backbench Liberal member of Parliament certainly was not a good or emotional speech. When commenting on good and emotional speeches, I must refer to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who led off the debate for this party a couple of days ago, and the speech made earlier this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Listening to speeches like that makes you proud to be a Canadian.
I have always been proud to be a Canadian. I am even more proud when I hear members responding to the wishes of Canadians. If anything has been missing in the context of a general debate on the Constitution, it is the fact that there has not been enough input from apolitical Canadians, those not affiliated with a political party. That is an important sector of our system as well. I refer to the individual Canadian who does not have the time to get involved. When I found out I would be taking part in this debate, I made it a point to hold public forums. These were held not only in the various areas of Halton in the last week or ten days, but, like the experience of most members, across Canada.
February 23, 1981

Today I do not intend to emphasize the technical analysis dealt with by previous speakers in a very proper and direct fashion. I want to bring to the floor of the House what I have been told by my constituents. I find that to be of great importance because a Member of Parliament is elected to abide by the wishes of the majority of his constituents. I have always felt that way. That is my feeling on this issue as on previous issues.
I know my speech will be cut at five o'clock for private members' hour. Before that time arrives, I wish to stress that opposition to the Liberal constitutional package is from the Canadian people, not just the interested groups, the eight provincial premiers and a number of New Democratic Party Members of Parliament. The opposition is from the majority of Canadians. Every poll, householder and other source shows that to be the fact.
Responses to a questionnaire in my constituency indicate that 83.1 per cent support patriation of the Constitution as it now is in Westminster. Only 18 per cent of those feel the provinces should be excluded. In other words, only 18 per cent support the Liberal motion. A Gallup poll in January showed that 64 per cent of Canadians opposed the Trudeau proposition and 22 per cent supported it. That was in January. We are now near the end of February. As hon. members know, the longer this debate goes on, the more support Canadians show toward the position of this party on patriation of the Constitution. The Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses asked their membership of 55,000 whether they were in favour or against. These are businessmen from across the country, including Quebec, the maritimes, the west Ontario. Seventy-five per cent opposed the Liberal position.
Canadians want the Constitution returned to Canada, but not in the way the Liberals are proposing. I have before me something which has been read into the record on a number of occasions; I think I have time to read it one more time. On October 22, the Leader of the Opposition moved the following motion:
That this House supports the immediate patriation of the Constitution of Canada, incorporating only the generally agreed upon amending formula known as the Vancouver consensus, so that all other constitutional changes shall be made in Canada by Canadians.
Canadians support that motion. Why cannot we, the elected representatives, Liberal, New Democratic or Conservative, act in this House of Commons on behalf of the majority of Canadians?
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Surrey-White Rock-North Delta) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reorganizing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by dividing its present responsibilities to provide for the establishment of two separate and distinct Crown corporations, one which will deal with all programming and distribution aspects and another which will be responsible for production.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion deals with the subject of the Crown corporation known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Whenever this topic comes before any general audience, it tends to raise the level of interest of CBC-philes and CBC-phobes. There are extremities of view on this particular subject. There are those who think there is very little wrong with the CBC and therefore only fine tuning-if I can use that metaphor in this context-is necessary to improve that corporation. Then there are those who are absolutely opposed to anything the CBC does and would like to see it sold or disbanded-anything just to get it off the corporate landscape of Canada.
I have been interested in the work of the CBC for quite some time, partly because of my background. My academic training is in the arts. I have an inherent interest in the arts. I am very concerned about the value structure in our society, and television and radio are the great communicators of values in our country.
February 23, 1981

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
Let me say parenthetically that I have been critical of the CBC many times. I am sure that often my criticism has been interpreted as CBC bashing when it was not intended to be that at all. I want hon. members to understand now that the motion before us is not to be used for CBC bashing. It is to be used so that we can look at the corporate structure for which we in Parliament are accountable. We can analyse it, hopefully somewhat dispassionately, and see if there are not perhaps better ways of dealing with these matters.
In March, 1980, an article entitled "Focus" was published in a magazine called Report. The article was written by Pierre Lortie. Mr. Lortie is the executive vice president and partner of the Montreal organized research firm SECOR Incorporated. He is a widely read author on economic matters. He received his bachelor's degree at Laval University and studied as well at Louvain, Belgium. He was executive assistant to the Quebec minister of finance from 1970 to 1972. He has also advised the government on urban transit and taught at Laval University. I would say that this man has fairly good credentials. I think he has all the right credentials to make some commentary on government organization and government corporations.
He argues that we ought to sell the CBC, presumably to the private sector, perhaps dismember it in some way or other and allow other communications industries to buy up those segments of CBC after it has been dismembered. That is not my argument. I underscore that that is not my argument, but Mr. Lortie makes the point that it ought to be sold for a very important reason, and that is that its original mandate is no longer necessary. He says that the CBC was founded by an act of Parliament in 1932 to establish and consolidate an infant communications industry in Canada. I will quote from Mr. Lortie's article as follows:
A cursory overview of the rapidly-expanding technology in telecommunications leaves the curious feeling that the CBC has outlived its usefulness. One can no longer seriously argue the case for development of an "infant industry" where the radio and television broadcasting industries are concerned: both are mature.
Foreign ownership is not a problem. Some might complain about the proportion of foreign programming. But we know from experience that public ownership and millions of dollars in subsidies to a Crown corporation do not solve this problem. The CRTC reported in 1977 that "to maintain a commercial presence and keep a share of the audience, CBC offers a high percentage of U.S. entertainment programming during prime time." More precisely, according to the report, 64 per cent of prime time fare consists of U.S.-made programs. Here it looks as though it is easier to preach about virtue than live with its predicaments.
Then he goes on to say that the prime industries are no longer radio and television but are industries such as pay-television, STV, fibre optics and satellite-to-cable television. Those are the infant industries today, not television as we know it.
Second, he says the function of the CBC was to establish the industry in all communities of Canada to bring that medium to all communities of Canada. I think all members of the House know that that has not happened, in spite of such programs as the accelerated coverage program. Mr. Lortie goes on to say:
We have seen that the major impetus for establishing the CBC or enlarging its mandate was the need to develop a Canadian broadcasting system while the
"industry" was still in its infancy. Furthermore, it was asserted that a public broadcasting corporation is required to provide service to small communities and remote areas. On the face of it, the last argument is compelling. Yet, if you hail from a small community in Quebec, your personal experience should leave you wondering. For example, the TV stations in Chicoutimi, Rimouski, Sherbrooke and Rouyn-Noranda are owned by private investors, often local citizens, not by the CBC. However, the CBC does own powerful TV stations in Montreal and Quebec City. In view of its fundamental mission, the network established by the CBC warrants a general examination.
The point is, of course, that the CBC has been great in establishing itself in major centres, but it has taken a long time to move out into the perimeter areas of Canada. I think particularly hon. members from Quebec know how factual that statement is.
However, regardless of what Mr. Lortie says in his article and regardless of how persuasive his argument is, that is not my point today. My argument is that we ought to split the CBC down the middle into two corporations. One should deal with programming and distribution, and the other one should deal with production. The issue is not whether we ought to have a public corporation. The issue is how efficient that particular corporation is.
I might add that my argument for splitting it already has some precedents because I think hon. members know that the original act which created the CBC and subsequent acts included another mandate which is not the CBC's today, and that is the mandate to be the regulatory agency for the communications industry in Canada. It used to be what we now call the CRTC. That was part of its job, but Parliament and the industry realized that that was no longer relevant to its job and that there was a massive conflict of interest in that respect. Therefore, Parliament cut off that particular responsibility. I am sorry to say an aspect of it still exists in the present act whereby the CBC is charged to advise the CRTC on matters of the industry. But the issue is one of efficiency.
I should like to refer to the Lambert commission report which was published approximately two years ago. It examined efficiency in government spending and indicated the following:
-accountability is the fundamental prerequisite for preventing the abuse of delegated power and for ensuring, instead, that power is directed toward the achievement of broadly accepted national goals with the greatest possible degree of efficiency, effectiveness, probity and prudence.
That is the job. Hon. members will know that the operating budget of the CBC today is about $1.5 million per day, or over $500 million a year in tax dollars. There is at least one reason for the tremendous cost of operating the CBC.
I put a question on the order paper which was answered on June 3 by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Stollery). One of the questions in question No. 1,025 was:
How many individuals are employed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the (a) English (i) television (ii) radio (b) French (i) television (ii) radio networks?
I wonder if hon. members have a ball park understanding of the number of permanent employees in the CBC. In the
February 23, 1981

French and English networks, radio and television, plus those who are operating in ancillary forums around the Ottawa area, there are 12,035 permanent employees.
Is that just in Ottawa?

No, these are across Canada. The fourth part of my question was:
How many individuals were employed by the CBC on a contract basis in (a) 1979 (b) 1980 to date-
Of course it referred to the French and English television and radio networks. In 1979 there were 30,817 persons on contract, and by 1980 the figure was 32,189. In other words, in one year the number of employees on a contract basis had grown by 1,372. That increase cost us something like $5.5 million.
At the same time the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) put a question on the Order Paper which was answered on October 7. His question was similar to the one I asked. The second part of his question was:
How many persons are regularly employed by the CBC on a contract basis?
Here is the conundrum: in answer to my question, the parliamentary secretary indicated 32,189, but in answer to the question of the hon. member for Vaudreuil it was 1,085. There is a lot of spillage or leakage somewhere, which can easily happen. The only difference between our questions was that he used the word "regularly." Are we to say, then, that 31,000 are irregular, or are we to say that there has been an awful ballooning in one year of 31,000 people employed by the CBC on a contract basis? There is something wrong.
Then the hon. member asked the following question:
How many persons receiving an annual salary from CBC also receive contract payments for specific assignments?
Of course that referred to moonlighting within the corporation, and the answer was that 412 were on regular salaries within the CBC and also moonlighting and receiving contract payment.
My point is that one cannot expect a corporation with approximately 44,000 employees, which is really the size of the city of Chatham or some other small city, to operate efficiently; there is a lot of spillage in that size of corporation.
We ought to split the corporation into two separate organizations. We hope this will create some competition which would plug some of the holes through which the leaks are taking place. Competition is always related to efficiency, or vice versa. So, I propose one separate corporation dealing with production facilities. Those facilities ought to be available by contract to independent and CBC producers on a fee for service basis. An independent producer would then be able to go into those facilities and say, "I want to rent these facilities for a production I have in mind; I am willing to pay the going rate." That corporation should be managed on a cash and value of production basis; CBC producers should pay the same amount as independent producers; then there will be some control of the costs.
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
The second corporation would deal with programming distribution. That CBC distribution centre would design its programs on the available ones from independent or CBC producers. It would buy those programs on a budget and value criteria. Because of the market system, hopefully it would find programs produced by independent producers to be just as attractive-and sometimes even maybe even more attractive- as those produced by CBC producers. The marketing division of the separate program distribution corporation would treat independent and CBC producers on an equal basis. In that way there would be an opportunity for CBC production costs to be held in line, because it could not have massive cost overruns and find a product which would be saleable to the distribution corporation. Therefore, CBC producers would have to discipline themselves in producing their programs. Also it would open up the entire area of distribution and viewing opportunities for a host of independently produced programs which ought to be seen but are possibly being shut out, because it is too easy for a bias to exist within the CBC against anything produced outside of the corporation.
I believe my proposal deserves some study. It is not an idea which will be bought overnight. I am sure the people within the CBC will fight it because they have a vested interest. I suggest to hon. members that there would be greater opportunities for parliamentary control of the vast expenditure of $1.5 million per day in the CBC today, for which we are accountable, if there were two independent corporations competing for the marketplace and providing what I think would be a higher quality of viewing for Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member made some very legitimate and good points. However, I question his modus operandi.
The "however" came too early.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I put it to the hon. member that there are now two distinct parts to the CBC. There is CBC Radio Canada and CBC in English Canada and there is talk of a CBC-2. In essence, we would have a CBC-1 and 2 in English Canada and a CBC-1 and 2 in French Canada. Thus, there are four units. The hon. member suggests that this be broken into production and distribution. In essence, he is talking about chopping CBC up into eight distinct units. If he is looking for more efficiency and more accountability, and I am quoting him, then I suggest that is not the way to do it. I think what he should be looking for-and I say this sincerely-is the good in CBC. He should be promoting that. I suggest it is more difficult, politically, to do such things. I will give an example, namely Louis Riel. It was a good production, it taught Canadians-
It was run three times in three years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
It taught Canadians right across Canada something about their country. It was entertaining. But it cost $2

February 23, 1981
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation million. Would the hon. member opposite say we need at least a dozen of these productions every two years, or one every two months? Would he suggest we spend $24 million? I hardly think so.
I think what he is doing is what is popular, and what I did for many years, that is, CBC bashing. It is almost as good as bureaucrat bashing. As top officials of the CBC say, "We are loved where we are not, and we are hated where we are." There is much truth in that.
What is CBC and how does it relate to this proposal? The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Fries-en) has placed before the House a very important motion concerning the two major functions of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that is, program production and program distribution. The motion, in essence, proposes the examination of the advisability of re-organizing the CBC into two separate and distinct Crown corporations, one having responsibility for production and the other being primarily involved in the distribution of programs it would acquire, purchase or negotiate from the production facility. The theory behind this is not new. If the hon. member will read "Touchstone", I think he will see that is exactly what the president of the CBC wants to do.
Not "Touchstone", but "Tombstone".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: The president of the CBC is talking about getting more Quebec people involved in production. He talks about better programming. I ask you what the other television networks are doing? Global has financial difficulties. What is CTV doing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Zero.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
That is right, zero. CTV is owned by a series of very lucrative affiliates. What they do is give just enough to the network, just enough to make it break even without doing top-notch production. They do some production, but not much. What is ATV doing? It is looking inward and not looking at all at Canada. Most of its production is designed to look inward. I say to the hon. member opposite that the only network doing anything of any importance and any quality is the CBC.
By the way, the hon. member is wrong with respect to the number of employees. He is 742 short. There are now 12,777, and holding. This is an updated figure.
The matter of two separate and distinct organizations to perform these functions must be examined in the light of past development and future options for the growth and health of public broadcasting in Canada. It must be looked at in the context of the utilization of public funds. What we have done with the CBC is to have set it up a decade or so ago and we have said that it must provide facilities to all towns with a population of over 500, all little villages with populations of over 500 and all little inlets with populations of over 500. They must bring CBC to the Eskimos and to all areas which the other networks will not serve. They have done this. But it has
cost a lot of money. Most of the money has gone into hardware.
Consequently, having followed the mandate of Parliament, they are now being criticized for bringing CBC to all areas of Canada. What they are looking for now is exactly what the hon. member has said-a production base. To create this production base in English Canada, they need the equivalent of what they put into Montreal. I challenge the hon. member opposite to put forward a motion in support of a production centre in Toronto. I say to him that he does not have the courage to do that, because if he did, he would find many people who would support him. He knows that such a production centre would cost $200 million. Is the hon. member suggesting that a production centre be built in Toronto at a cost of $200 million? That is exactly what it would cost.
We have given many mandates to the CBC. They have had to go to Regina, Victoria and New Brunswick, where there was no CBC until this year. They are just moving into New Brunswick. They have made their plans. They have announced that it will take some time for them to establish themselves there. The CBC is also in Sudbury. They are in these places because of the demands of Members of Parliament. The CBC having done all these things, it is now being criticized for using funds to follow the mandate of this Parliament. If this is an error, it is the result of our perception of Canada. It is not hardware which is needed, it is better quality Canadian programming.
Oddly enough, I was out in the hon. member's province as a CRTC commissioner. That was my last hearing. We were dealing with a presentation from a large B.C. delegation which was saying that they were receiving five U.S. channels in their area. They said that was undemocratic and that they were entitled to receive six. There were 10,000 buttons distributed by well-meaning British Columbians which said "CRTC, CBC-Get out of B.C." The slogan rhymed-that is culture.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. 1 cannot let the hon. member's comment in this regard go by. It was not this side of the House which published those buttons, but the former Liberal member for Vancouver-Kingsway who was peddling them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Over the years the CBC has been the most effective channel through which to address the matter of Canadian program development. Again, this was primarily due to the small Canadian population base, as well as the accompanying and persistent constraints on production and distribution.
In the Canadian private sector, we have one of the best production facilities in North America. It is called Glen Warren Productions, which is situated in Toronto. It is part of the CTV empire, for want of a better word. Why is that facility not used?

It is for Americans.
February 23, 1981

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: As the hon. member says, it does American productions which are sold to the United States. And that illustrates the attitude of the private sector. It is an attitude which the CBC must fight. If I understand correctly what the hon. member opposite has said, he is suggesting that we should build more facilities-
No, no.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Let me finish, please. The hon. member is saying we should build more public facilities which the private sector can use.
Keep the ones you have.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: He wants more public facilities that the private sector can use, or ones that we already have, so that they can use their facilities for United States productions. What kind of subsidy is that?
What is the difference between selling that and selling lumber?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
The CBC has always been a prime mover in Canadian program development but, at the request of Parliament, it has also figured highly in the extension of the broadcast distribution facilities.
We must make up our minds today, or within the next year, whether there will be a CBC at all. Right now in Ontario there are 56 American stations coming into the province. I firmly believe that you should not watch Canadian programs just because they are Canadian. You should watch Canadian programs because they are a good quality product. We, as parliamentarians, must decide today whether we will put our money where our mouth is and give the CBC the necessary funds to carry out this type of programming.
Obviously, we are producing good actors, writers, comedians, people in drama, because they are showing up in California. We must be doing something right in Canada because these people are coming out. In the words of Northrup Frye, they are thrown up from their environments. We are producing these people in all parts of Canada; but at the head end, namely, the House of Commons, we are not giving the required support to the CBC and its production in terms of the dollars necessary to keep these people in Canada and not let them escape to the United States. If we did, then we would be able to produce quality prognms which, first, would be watched by Canadians and, second, could be sold on the world market.
You don't want to export them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
We want to export them, Mr. Speaker; CBC wants to export them; the private sector wants to export them. They are not being exported because they are not being bought; and they are not being bought because they are not good enough; and they are not good enough because we will not put the dollars into them.
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
Wait until Andrew Johnson reads this.
Alan.
Sorry, A1 Johnson.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
In addition to the competition from which we are suffering, primarily the United States-there is not that much coming in from Europe-the CBC has another problem. It is seriously challenged today by cabletelevision, pay TV, closed circuit delivery systems. Do you know what these are? They are supposed to result in an expansion of culture, but they are really one more way of hustling the American product, one more way of making a dollar, and one more way of defeating our own Canadian culture by not supporting it. Besides that, they are suffering from the adverse effects of optical fibre technology, of the videodiscs on the market, of the satellites. For $420, you can buy a dish which you just set up and point south. You lift it 18 or 19 degrees above the surface, and you can receive almost 21 or 22 U.S. programs. This is all new in the last three or four years.
The CBC was suffering before that. Prior to that time, other than sports, news and specials, it had a watch factor of perhaps 10 per cent. Over all, with these factors, it would have had a watch factor of, perhaps, 20 per cent. In other words, before these came onto the market, 25 per cent to 30 per cent of the time we were watching Canadian television, and 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the time we were watching U.S. broadcasting. It was worse in English Canada. It was far better in French Canada.
Let's build a wall.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
But they are suffering too, from exposure to the culture from the United States. It is far worse now with the satellites, the videodiscs and the various technologies which have come on the market.
The point is that the whole on-air broadcasting and on-air culture is more fragile today than it was three or four years ago. Even though it is politically popular today to attack the CBC as if it were in the best interests of Canada, I do not think it is constructive any more. The CBC is on the ropes, and Canadians must decide whether the corporation is going to bind this country together, in the broadcasting sense, or whether we are going to keep it on the ropes and drive it right out of the ring, because it can be done. People listen to what is said in the House of Commons, and if we say irresponsible things- and I do not suggest that what you are saying is irresponsible-they are going to be taken as the truth, and if they are taken as the truth, people are going to turn even more against the CBC. There will come a point in this House of Commons, if people do not periodically try to defend what the CBC is trying to do, when there will be a vote, and there may be sufficient numbers in this House to vote to disband CBC, and then what are we going to do, watch ABC, CBS? Perhaps we could watch educational television from the United States? That time is nigh. Just listen to what the hon. member has said, because he makes some good points; but carry it one step

February 23, 1981
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation further and give the CBC the support that it deserves and merits. After all, it is not doing it for its own benefit. It is doing it for the benefit of Canadians across this country. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) that consideration be given to dividing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation into two, with completely separate jurisdictions over program production and distribution, provides fruit for argument both for the status quo and for change. The test of a final decision, I believe, is whether such a move would improve control and promote progress in these areas, and, of course, whether or not such a move would prove cost-effective.
In establishing some framework for efficiency, it should be pointed out that the corporation has a good record of performance. Studies have demonstrated that the CBC is an efficient and productive organization compared with other public broadcasters. The conclusion drawn from the studies is that the CBC has produced more programming in radio and television with less public funding and fewer employees than the BBC, or the networks of France and Japan. In fact, the CBC produces more than twice as many hours of programming per employee than other public broadcasters, in both television and radio.
I think that if you are a fan of radio, the way I am, then you, Mr. Speaker, along with other members of this House, would agree that the quality of CBC radio is unsurpassed in North America at the present time.
Right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
CBC radio has been worked upon over the recent years, and has developed to be not only informative, but extremely enjoyable.
The CBC is demonstrably one of the most efficient, if not the most efficient, program production houses in the world, doing more with less than any other national public broadcaster. Much of this is done by a competent, talented staff aided by external contributions.
In terms of efficient use of funds, the CBC's costs per hour of programming are substantially lower than those of other public broadcasters. The total budget per hour of CBC's production output in 1975-76 was $11,600 for television compared with $43,500 for the BBC, $56,200 for the Swedish service and $78,400 for the French system.
From these statistics, the conclusion can be drawn that the CBC's ratio of program and distribution expenditures to administrative expenditures compared favourably with those of the private broadcasting sector, a conclusion which was at that time supported by the analyses of the private broadcasting sector done by Statistics Canada.
The CBC has taken a conscious managerial decision to increase greatly its involvement with the independent production sector. Its involvement embraces a number of areas;
namely, procurement of programs from independent producers, commissioning productions, co-financing and co-producing arrangements with independent producers, and craft support including post-production houses, like film processing labs and sound recording studios, as well as script development. Indeed, whenever CBC and Radio-Canada schedules can be complemented by such material, effort is made to include independent Canadian productions. It should be noted, however, that competition and private sector productions are not necessarily synonymous with lower production costs, or that private producers do not incur cost overruns.
I would say that the CBC has a record of assisting, where possible, the independent producers in carrying out their tasks. 1 am sure you have noted, Mr. Speaker, that people have complained there are many more employees of CBC present when press conferences are called than people from other networks and they want to know whether this is necessary. It should be noted, however, that the independent producers, the competing networks, make use of the equipment set up by the CBC. Certainly the costs of the independent producers would be considerably higher were it not for the fact that the CBC supplies a good deal of the necessary equipment.
A brief analysis of the situation in the United States makes this point quite clear. The major United States networks do relatively little in-house production, other than news, current affairs programming and sports. The bulk of the variety and drama productions comes from independent producers in Los Angeles and New York City. The structure of the United States industry is not without its costs. Having selected scripts for pilots, a network will pay what essentially amounts to a "licence fee", which today is usually less than the actual cost of making the pilot. In that market, it is the producer who absorbs the difference, with the hope of making it up on rights for syndication, foreign sales and literary rights.
The point made here is that, even in the United States, producers seldom cover their costs on a production. Cost overruns are either guaranteed outright by the networks in the manner of "overage" payments or the producer gambles on a long syndication run. There are built-in inefficiencies in all systems but what counts in the United States is the large market base and the potential for the recovery of costs, along with sizeable profits. In Canada, the marketplace is much different. Production funds must be utilized efficiently to achieve optimal results.
To some degree, we have already seen the corporation's efficiency in responding to its program production mandate and its flexibility and willingness to seek out the services of the Canadian independent production sector. This clearly has a stimulative effect on this service industry sector. Also, the single organization concept for both the distribution and production functions has been found to be efficient. The corporation has been able to draw upon its over-all resources to respond to so challenging a mandate. The dual agency alterna-
February 23, 1981

tive appears to add nothing new to the present broadcasting system.
Other questions also, are raised about the corporation. Would the present organizational structure not be in a better position than two corporations to integrate within its ranks the changing objectives and functions of the CBC? In its long-range objectives, is the CBC not now well placed to exploit and to market the substantial expertise of skilled personnel, associated with the combined hardware and distribution side of the business for example, to Third World countries seeking our aid, as it frequently does? The issue of morale among all experienced and dedicated staff, too, must not be overlooked.
Furthermore, from the point of view of the over-all efficient use of public funds, it is difficult to imagine how two separate and distinct organizations would not add to the burden to be borne by Canadian taxpayers. From a purely administrative point of view, many of the present functions would be duplicated since, depending on the structure of the organization itself, separate boards of directors and management functions would have to be established if the organizations were to function properly. Other questions, such as co-operation between the two organizations, duplicate roles regarding contracts with industry, governments and regulators also come to mind.
The CBC has an admirable performance record, and further, it has an unexcelled international reputation. Public broadcasting in Canada is superior in quality worldwide, relative to the financial support and human resources available. Separate and distinct organizations would not necessarily increase the efficiency and effectiveness of the services being provided and would, in all likelihood, cost more.
While I would not declare that the CBC has mounted the uppermost pinnacle of efficiency and can ascend no further, I believe it has coped well with developing requirements and is planning well to meet the future. My advice to the House, therefore, is don't tamper with success!

Mr. Speaker, fairly often we hear the Progressive Conservative Party requesting the government to cut down the number of Crown corporations in this country. So it is a bit of a change today when the hon. member asks that two corporations be created where one is doing the job. I do not hear my hon. friend advocating that private broadcasters should break themselves into separate corporations, one side for production and the other side for programming. Frankly, this is an idea we have heard in the past and not found acceptable, so we see no reason to support the motion that is before the House today.
I do not criticize the hon. member for bringing in a motion that calls for a discussion of broadcasting generally and for a discussion of the CBC. Perhaps we could do this more often. I am prepared to say that in my view the CBC, for all its faults-and it has them not only in broadcasting but in labour relations, and so on-is nevertheless doing a good job in Canada. It is a unifying force, an institution for Canadianism, and I think we should give it our full support.
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
In my view, the proposal in the motion does not go in that direction, and therefore I hope the House will not pass it this afternoon but that instead, there will be other expressions of support by members of this House of Commons for a very useful and worth-while institution in this country, the CBC.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Stollery (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Fries-en) and others. Although the purpose of the motion is pretty clear, that the hon. member would like to see the CBC made into two corporations, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has just explained the sense behind it, the point of it escapes me. The arguments of the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta, which I have heard on these kinds of subjects for many years, give me no clue as to why he would be interested in creating two Crown corporations instead of one. Given his philosophical view of these things, I am puzzled as to why he would be interested in creating yet another layer of bureaucracy. I am sure many people would argue, as he would, that one of the problems with Crown corporations is that they are weighted with bureaucracy. His argument that we should create a special bureaucracy to take the place of the CBC, therefore puzzles me. It does not seem to make any sense to me. I would also point out to the hon. member that when he discusses the CBC, he seems to take the view-and in this regard he has associated himself with other motions-that there should be unlimited access to signals from outside of the country. I am sure the hon. member is interested in more productions being done in Canada, because I presume that is the only substantive argument he is putting forward in favour of this motion. But I do not understand how this can come from an hon. member who believes in freedom of information and in signals being allowed across borders. He seems to take the view that that is something with which there should be very little interference. Canadian production, CBC and private, already has difficulty in competing with U.S. networks which think nothing of spending half a million dollars per hour on production. In Canada, the only serious production house, namely the CBC, spends $100,000. In other words, Canadian production is outspent five to one by the competition.
The hon. member would now like to see a special Crown corporation put together to take care of production. At the same time he does not want to give protection to the existing facilities in Canada. The sort of protection that may well be needed, in view of the technological changes, was explained to him by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin). The arguments which he put forward appear to be contrary to his previous approach to the problems of broadcasting in Canada.
[ Translation\
-Mr. Speaker, in short the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta has proposed that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as it now exists be replaced by two distinct

February 23, 1981
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation Crown corporations which would be fully independent from an administrative standpoint. That is what he has proposed. One corporation would be responsible for programming and the other for distribution. I must say that there is no mention of the CBC technical problems which are more complicated than a simple distribution operation.
Those problems have cost a bundle to the Canadian taxpayers because of the technical means the CBC representatives have to use. And as the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie was saying, they have just now approached the problems of northern New Brunswick which is one of the under served areas of Canada, and the cost of survival in Canadian regions where there are very few people. First I would like to give this motion a short historic background. Then I will weigh the pros and cons of that proposal in light of the technological challenge of the 1980s. Or I might leave that task to my colleague from Manicouagan (Mr. Maltais) who perhaps may want to speak to this motion for a few minutes.
Whether we are talking about the English or the French network, with all their hesitations and their evolution which mirrors the development of Canada over the last quarter century, the history of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation spells success. And yet the corporation has had to overcome serious obstacles, including the breadth of the territory and the dispersion of the Canadian population, as in New Brunswick for instance. The very economy of television production is an even more serious obstacle because from the outset it militates against the production of Canadian programming. American competition is so strong indeed that some people have said that Canada's radio-television system has become ever more a means of recycling American broadcasts. Those obstacles appear to be almost insurmountable since the funds at the disposal of the American networks are two to three times larger than those available to the Canadian networks. In addition, the Canadian networks can buy low cost American programs and get more advertising dollars than they would for a Canadian program. Finally, through the cable distribution system, Canadian viewers can tune in to a great many programs aired by American stations.

I will end my remarks at this point because I know there is another hon. member who would like to say a few words on this subject.

Mr. Speaker, a while ago, I was astonished to hear my colleague from the opposition ask that the CBC be divided into two entirely separate entities. As pointed out the former speaker, I feel the problem with CBC, at this time, is one of consolidation. To my mind, we can say that all in all, the CBC has been a great success. Just think of how vast and diverse is the territory it covers! It is a challenge that not even the American network could have met with such a small population as is the case in Canada.
As my time is very limited, I should like to stress one point only, the responsibility the CBC has to try to increase the Canadian and even the regional content of its broadcasts. That, to some extent, is the problem which confronts the Canadian people in terms of identifying the contents of its own network. Why should Canadians often prefer American or foreign programs? Because, within the contents of our CBC broadcasts, either in French or in English, there is often a feeling that programs are a copy or a remake of other programs that have nothing particularly Canadian about them.
In the area I represent, our main difficulty with the CBC concerns regional programming. In that regard, the minister was very firm recently when he said it was imperative for the CBC to move toward regional productions, that people might identify themselves with the content of their own network. One thing is sure: with the limited financial resources we grant the CBC, because after all our resources are limited-which often is not the case at the creation level-we do have to make choices.
However, in view of the main objective of the CBC and the difficulty of meeting this objective, in view of the terms of reference given to the corporation, I believe that it can be said that it has had a major success. We should consolidate further before thinking of dividing up the network. I am really surprised to hear my colleague opposite talk about dividing the network and having two separate units since his colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), appeared like myself before the CRTC to object to CBC II and Tele II.
I believe that the CBC should not aim for an extended mandate at the present time, but should instead try to consolidate what it now has. I believe that all Canadians would be proud of an increased quality and unity in the contents of CBC programming. This is one of the major objectives of the CBC at the present time as a Canadian network, and we must do everything, not to divide the CBC, but rather to unify it and to ask it to consolidate its present assets to look further to the future.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hour provided for the consideration of private members' business has now expired. Accordingly, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
February 23, 1981

The House resumed debate on the motion of Mr. Chretien, seconded by Mr. Roberts, for an Address to Her Majesty the Queen respecting the Constitution of Canada.
And on the amendment of Mr. Epp, seconded by Mr. Baker (Nepean-Carleton)-That the motion be amended in Schedule B of the proposed resolution by deleting Clause 46, and by making all necessary changes to the Schedule consequential thereto.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. When the debate was interrupted at five o'clock p.m., the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, before the private members' hour I stressed to hon. members the importance of listening to the people at the grass roots, something that many of us, primarily the Liberals opposite, have not done enough of, particularly when it comes to the constitutional debate. My public forums in the constituency of Halton, at Acton, Milton and Oakville, were well attended. The people there were representative of other parts of Canada. They really let me hear what they thought about the Constitution.
Without a doubt, they want the Constitution here. In fact, it should have been here years ago, but certainly not in the package that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberals introduced before this House and in the manner they introduced it.
People ask me why this Parliament has been preoccupied for nearly a year with the constitutional debate, virtually ignoring the important issues. That is the question. This was made clear to me in October of last year when I sent a questionnaire to my constituents. I asked them, "What, in your opinion, are the most important issues in Canada today?" The replies were as follows: inflation, 47.1 per cent; energy, 14.3 per cent; unemployment, 9 per cent; law and order, 8.1 per cent, and so on down the line until the Constitution, 3.5 per cent.
The results of this constituency poll, as hon. members know, were verified by a recent Gallup poll which clearly indicated that the majority of Canadians still consider inflation the number one problem, unemployment close behind, and the Constitution way down the line.
In the public forums where I speak in my travels across Canada I am asked why the elected representatives are preoccupied with this situation at this time when we are facing inflation at 12 per cent, unemployment of one million or more, and bankruptcies, the largest portion of which occur in the small business sector of our economy. In 1980 alone, they accounted for some $700 million in liabilities. That is a shocking increase when one considers that only ten short years ago the total dollar value was only $300,000.
The Constitution
Real wages in 1980 increased by 9.9 per cent, only to be eroded by a 15.2 per cent increase in the price of food. Almost two million person-days were lost as a result of strikes and lockouts in the last three months of 1980. The national debt soared to a projected $14 billion this year. These are some of the concerns about which Canadians ask me, their elected representative. I am sure they are asking the Liberal members as well.
Any sincere attempt to develop a true people's package, as the Prime Minister refers to it, not a Constitution package, should address itself to the real concerns of the Canadian people, those I have just stated. It would propose, not the removal of the constitutional guarantee to own property, for example, which is something I want to touch on a little later but, rather, fuel and shelter allowances or a mortgage rebate plan. It would demonstrate a willingness to come to an energy agreement with Alberta. It would spell out a national energy plan which would incorporate the wisdom of the business community rather than the philosophic edicts of bygone colleagues.
Having said that and having articulated what I know are the major concerns and priorities of the citizens of this nation, I would like to turn to the issue of patriation. My colleagues have referred to this before me, but I want to put something on record again because it is important to say it over and over so that the Liberals will go back to their ridings, listen to their people and come back to the House of Commons representing the wishes of their people. When the vote comes before this Parliament, I hope they will vote in a non-partisan way and on behalf of their constituents.
It would be convenient for the Prime Minister for political reasons to define positions on this resolution as being either for or against it. This distorted perception needs to be clarified again because clearly the government is making every attempt to tag those who do not go along with his constitutional proposals as being colonials. This is just another example of the Prime Minister's contempt of the Canadian people and another example of what he hopes will be a successful attempt to mislead a misinformed and manipulated multitude into overlooking the inadequacies of his package and to distort the efforts of those concerned about the dangerous precedents which will be set should this proposal proceed as the Prime Minister has planned. It is because of regard for the federalist principles upon which this nation has been founded and upon which assurances our provinces, partners, contracted into this federation that we are determined that no constitutional amendments that would create third-class provinces and give a permanent veto to central Canada will be accepted. The Prime Minister knows this. He also knows that the package as it now stands would never receive a consensus in Canada. This is why he is going to Westminster, not just to have the Constitution patriated, for there is a number of simple ways of proceeding with such a revision, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said earlier today. The Prime Minister is going to Westminster with the hope that the British government will

February 23, 1981
The Constitution
see fit to pass what he knows will be unacceptable to the Canadian federation. In short, he has a separate set of rules for his favourite amendments. It is the Right Hon. Prime Minister who is the colonialist when he speaks this way.
I do not think it is unreasonable that we on this side of the House have asked that the convention of a century of Parliaments be recognized and the sovereignty of the provincial legislatures be recognized. This is what the Vancouver consensus proposes should be done. We know there is agreement throughout Canada for this process. We also know by instinct that no one man has the right to change our nation, to disregard convention or to destroy our federation just because he chooses to do so. Nor is it unreasonable to begin with the position that agreement can indeed be reached rather than assume that such is not possible.
The Prime Minister would like us to think that our federation has not worked. Many others before me have reminded us that it indeed has. Federal-provincial agreements have often been reached in the past. I refer, for example, to medicare, the Canada Pension Plan and equalization, to name a few. Agreements will continue to be reached in this country in the future, but not with the passage of the proposal before us. That is one of the reasons why Canadians disagree with this over-all proposal.
I know all members have received all sorts of letters from their constituents. I would like just to quote a few excerpts from the many letters which we have received, all opposing the resolution. I challenge a Liberal Member of Parliament to tell me that his constituents, in writing, through phone calls or by questionnaires such as the one I put to my constituents, agree with his proposals. In other words, I am suggesting that hon. members opposite will be voting against the wishes of their own constituents.
Oh, oh!
We always wake them up when we tell the truth. That hurts them the most. It happens every time. Here is a letter from a constituent in Calgary.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) has the floor.

The following is a quotation from a letter from a Canadian to me.
Trudeau is bent on changing this country into a socialized dictatorship and you are the only people who can stop this fool ... He is dividing the country to conquer it.
That is from Robert Moyer of Calgary. Here is part of another letter:
Equal application of discriminatory rights is not the answer.
That is from Judy Alexander of Oakville. Here is another one:
If Pierre changes our Constitution and then brings it home, what he is bringing home is not our Constitution but Pierre's Constitution. We are led to believe there is nothing we can do to stop this changed Constitution from arriving in Canada because Pierre was voted into power by a majority.
That is signed by Margaret Catchpole of Oakville. There is a point in that. This Canadian citizen voted for the Liberals, perhaps, but she did not give the Liberal government the mandate which the Prime Minister says he has in dealing with the Constitution. I did not hear him make great waves during the election campaign about the constitutional proposals and what he would do. In fact, I did not hear him say anything during the election campaign. However, what did remind me of his campaign promises in the last election campaign were those of Premier Levesque of Quebec when he ran his last election campaign on the economy and not separatism but then reversed the situation.
I do not like quoting too much, but I must quote one part of an editorial for the benefit of the Liberal government, which is mostly comprised of Quebec members.
Oh, oh!

We have read many editorials from Ontario, from the western provinces and from the maritimes. Here is one from Le Devoir, which usually supports the Liberals. I will read just a portion of it, as follows:
If Mr. Trudeau wishes to be intellectually honest, he will recognize that he has no moral right to alter the federal system without consulting the country. Before going any further the Prime Minister should call a general election. It is essential that Canadians know clearly what future is being readied for them in Ottawa and London.
That is from an editorial in Le Devoir of October 16. There should be an election or even a referendum because when we are talking about the future of our country, the people should have a say, and they do not have a say when it comes to the benches opposite and to the majority of those left wingers to my left, with the exception of the four escapees and now their new supporter in Saskatchewan.
Allow me to become a little personal because this is relevant to this whole situation. My family and I escaped from a foreign country in which rights, privileges and freedoms were taken away. I speak of Czechoslovakia. There were five of us children and my parents. We left because we were bred on the strengths, opportunities and freedoms which used to exist in that country. When these disappeared, my father in his wisdom took the whole family, seven of us, out, with no money, to a new country where we could not speak the language. We did not know the new way of life in the new country. We came to the shores of Canada. Upon stepping onto the shores of Canada, I and my family fell in love with this country. We have loved this country dearly from the day we stepped onto its soil. It has given us many opportunities. It has given me opportunities in the fields of amateur sport, professional sport, business, the helping of disabled children, Big Brother organization and the list goes on. It was a country which provided the freedoms, hopes and aspirations of many Canadians like myself and my family. My reason for telling this story is very simple. We came to Canada because the freedoms were here-
February 23, 1981

the freedom to move, the freedom to speak, the freedom to work, and freedom of the press.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Oh, oh!

What does the hon. member opposite have to say about it? Why does he not rise and say what his constituents think about the Liberals opposing this? The Liberals are trying to tell me that Canada does not have these freedoms. They are trying to tell me that Canada has no freedoms, that we are not allowed to speak or to travel.
What happened in Czechoslovakia?
Now an hon. member opposite is telling me to go back to Czechoslovakia.
That is not what he said.
That is a good Liberal! In that sense, if we compare-

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. If the hon. member has not understood what we have said on this side of the House, I would advise him to read and pay attention to what we said previously. We would not want to see what happened in Czechoslovakia occur in Canada. This is what we said.
Hear, hear!
