subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE
CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 22, I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), in connection with Canada Savings Bonds, to be fair to the ordinary people of Canada and pay them an interest rate on their savings which would be appropriate to his high interest rate policy. At that time the minister said "-of course we intend to be fair to those who have purchased bonds." Since January 22, when I asked that question, the minister and the government have refused to be fair. At the present time, the interest paid on Canada Savings Bonds is 11.5 per cent. Just this week the government placed $700 million worth of ordinary bonds on the bond market at 13.75 per cent. A number of bond issues are presently selling with an interest rate in excess of 14 per cent and the government is paying pretty close to 17 per cent on its treasury bill indebtedness. It pays 13.5 per cent to the big insurance companies, the sophisticated lenders, and nearly 17 per cent to the big banks, those which can afford to buy treasury bills.
February 23, 1981

To the ordinary people of Canada, the people the government conned into buying Canada Savings Bonds as an investment in the country, the government pays 11.5 per cent. The ordinary people who bought their bonds because they were an investment in Canada, for some strange reason believed the propaganda put out by the government. Until now they also believed the minister when he said in this House, as reported at page 6449 of Hansard "-of course, we intend to be fair-."
What is fair about that when you can get 13 or 13.5 per cent at a bank, and when you can buy one year bills at a trust company and get 14 per cent or better? What is fair about the government's intention? The answer is, nothing. Since January 1, about a billion dollars worth of Canada Savings Bonds have been redeemed. Because interest is calculated on the first day of every month, there will be another massive redemption next week. My calculations show that $968 million worth of Canada Savings Bonds have been redeemed since January 1 and there will likely be massive redemptions after March 1, a Sunday.
It is not just the people of Canada with whom I ask the minister to be fair, in terms of investing in Canada Savings Bonds. These bonds are a very expensive way for the government to borrow money. In floating an issue, the government pays commissions equal to 1 per cent of the bonds. In addition, it pays for massive advertising, printing and other things involved in the cost of a bond issue.
The parliamentary secretary is in the House tonight to answer my question, and I suspect that he can confirm that the cost of raising money through Canada Savings Bonds is close to 1.5 per cent. The billion dollars worth of Canada Savings Bonds redeemed between January 1 and today represents a massive cost to all of us; not just to the people lending money at an inadequate rate of interest but to the whole of Canada, those who have to pay for inept financial management.
On January 22, I suggested to the minister that he raise the interest rate on Canada Savings Bonds to 12.5 per cent. The minister has not done that, so we continue to get massive CSB redemptions. According to the Bank of Canada statement dated February 19, year over year we have had $1,923 billion worth of Canada Savings Bonds redeemed. The minister said to me and to members in this House that it was because he intended to be fair. However, the minister refuses to be fair. He wants to be able to borrow the savings of Canadians and gyp them by telling them that they are getting a good deal. He does not want to give them what they can get in a bank account or a savings plan.
The government has an obligation to come clean with Canadians. It can either pay Canadians a fair rate of interest on their savings, or induce them into handing their money over to a government which does not even give them 12 per cent interest, which is the rate of inflation.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA SAVINGS BONDS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN INTEREST RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his question of January 22 to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen), the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn) noted that $261 million in Canada Savings Bonds were redeemed during the week ending January 14, 1981. In view of this rather high rate of CSB redemptions related to the high level of interest rates generally, the hon. member asked what the minister was prepared to do to reduce the future level of such redemptions. It was suggested that the government should be fair to CSB investors by increasing the rate of interest on these bonds.
I recognize that the 11.5 per cent 1981 CSB rate and the 10.5 per cent rate payable in the remaining years to maturity on all issues is somewhat lower than the current interest rates on other forms of government debt. However, it is not unusual for CSBs to have a slightly lower rate of return than other forms of government debt. Canada Savings Bonds compete in a different market. The CSB rate is guaranteed for a period of several years, whereas treasury bill rates, while attractive at this moment, may well move down sharply when short-term instrument yields change. Government of Canada marketable bonds, longer-term bonds, also have a more attractive yield at this moment than CSBs due to the market risks associated with these instruments. If interest rates move to higher levels, investors will suffer a capital loss when selling Canada marketable bonds, whereas Canada Savings Bonds can always be redeemed at full face value by the investor.
The government is continuously monitoring the level of interest rates payable on short-term savings instruments, and feels that in the present environment the yield on outstanding Canada Savings Bonds issues is still fair and reasonable. In most cases, the current rates payable on savings instruments which compete directly with CSBs have not changed dramatically since the interest rate on all issues was revised on November 3, 1980 to 11.5 per cent for the current year. The only major exception is the chartered bank non-chequable saving rate which has moved up by 3 percentage points since early November to the present 13.5 per cent. However, as most hon. members know, depositors are not guaranteed this rate for any stated period. It may go down as quickly as it went up. This is not the case with the rate on Canada Savings Bonds.
I am aware that some rates at present payable on longer-term savings instruments are also higher than those now payable on CSBs. However, in many cases these instruments cannot be redeemed before maturity. In others, redemption before maturity results in a stiff interest penalty, bringing the effective interest rate substantially below the current Canada Savings Bond rate. CSBs are a good investment. The rate currently being paid is a rate that is fair, given the flexibility which investors are offered with regard to the guaranteed face value and the ability to redeem these instruments at face value at the choice of the investor at any time.

February 23, 1981
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: ENVIRONMENT-POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
ENVIRONMENT-POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one by one legal efforts to block the controversial SCA pipeline from discharging chemical wastes into the Niagara River are dying in the courts. I am well aware of the efforts made by local environmental groups, the efforts of the previous member for Niagara Falls, Mr. Jake Froese, and of the great efforts made by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain) across the way. What he needs and must have is the support of his colleagues on that side of the House. Only top level negotiations and agreement between the highest authorities of both the United States and Canada will bring to a halt this SCA proposal. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during the election campaign of 1980 made a commitment to the people of Niagara through the hon. member for Niagara Falls that he would urge the U.S. authorities to prevent SCA from discharging chemical wastes into that river.
On February 19, in the absence of the Prime Minister I asked the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) exactly what steps the minister or his government had taken to urge the U.S. authorities to pressure SCA into discontinuing its proposal. The minister continues to avoid or refuses to answer or to admit that he cannot do anything about it or will not take any action to prevent this continuing or proposed discharge.
In the special report of the International Joint Commission, the recommendation was made that further dumping of those substances which have given rise to the high level of pollution be terminated. According to the IJC, neither the U.S. nor Canadian governments have met the 1978 pollution guidelines. The minister responded that he and the government do support the IJC, which must mean that they accept its recommendations. The question, therefore, is what the minister and his government are prepared to do in support of those recommendations.
We already know that the sewage disposal plant in Niagara Falls, New York is one of the pollutants of that river. There is no use in just saying it is one of the problems today. A question must be asked as to what is being done to pressure that municipality into remedying the waste problem.
Years ago sources of pollutants were identified and the proportions of pollutants established. Studies have been done, and recommendations have been made. The level of toxic chemicals, such as dioxin found in fish and gull eggs around the southern Lake Ontario region, is indeed shocking to all of us. According to officials of the state of New York, Lake Ontario fish contain the highest levels of dioxin in the world.
The minister declared that his position has not changed and, indeed, will remain the same. The question is what position the minister is advocating. The river is considered to be one of the most polluted in the entire North American continent. Over the last summer and fall it was learned that besides the massive amount of chemical waste making its way into the river, large amounts of explosives have also been discovered.
Local environmental groups and citizens on both sides of the border have expressed their fears and anger not only at the decision of the American courts but also the Canadian government's lack of a firm stand which could have had a positive influence on the U.S. authorities.
I therefore would like to ask the following question: what concrete action is the Minister of the Environment or the Canadian government prepared to take to have the recommendations of the IJC implemented? What communications has this government had with the U.S. government since the decisions of the New York courts were handed down on February 12, 1981?
If the present United States administration remains true to expectations, the likelihood is that pollution in the Niagara River will increase rather than decrease. The International Joint Commission has found that situation intolerable. The people of the Niagara region have found that situation intolerable. Hon. members opposite can join with the hon. member for Niagara Falls in impressing upon the minister that he must make it clear to the U.S. authorities that the present situation is not only unacceptable but also that certain specific, positive action must now be taken to impress upon them that this river is an international waterway and that there must be respect for it as such and for the people who live on both sides of that waterway.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENVIRONMENT-POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-REPRESENTATIONS TO UNITED STATES AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank my friend, the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), for having raised this issue on the late show. I believe it goes without saying that the government is concerned about the issue he addresses. It is an issue we have had occasion to talk much about in this House over recent months, and that is due in part to the continuing efforts of my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain), who has left no stone unturned in continuing to bring this to the attention of the department and the government. He is doing a good job with it, and he has the support of members on this side of the House. That is not the problem. I believe the hon. member for St. Catharines is just being mischievous when he says that might be the problem. That is not the problem at all.
Indeed, it is very easy to point the finger and, were I in a finger-pointing mood tonight, I would remind the hon. member for St. Catharines that while he is in the mood to enlist collaborative and co-operative effort, he should go out and enlist the efforts of his colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), who, as minister of the environment, refused to do anything on this particular issue. He did absolutely zilch. He did nothing on this issue. I remind the hon. member for St. Catharines of that. The record shows that.
While the hon. member for St. Catharines is in the mood for enlisting co-operative efforts, I invite him to go and see his provincial Tory colleague, Mr. Welch, who lives in the area.
February 23, 1981

He represents the area but he will not, mind you, drink the water. Mr. Welch has refused to do anything about it in his capacity of MNA with the Ontario government, nor has the gentleman who holds the position of minister of the environment in the Ontario government. He also has refused to do anything on this issue.
If the hon. member wants there to be co-operative effort and if he wants to point fingers, I can help him do a bit of both, but I suggest instead that he recognize that this is a problem which is of genuine concern to all of us. There is nothing to be gained by pointing fingers. Does the hon. member think for one fraction of a second that there is anybody in this House who wilfully goes out and encourages the further pollution of these waterways? That is the suggestion we hear tonight. We are all in this together, and I suggest to the hon. member for St. Catharines that we would all be a lot better off if we stopped pointing fingers and began examining what has been done.
Had I sufficient time remaining-the hon. member has seven minutes, but I only have three in which to respond-I would tell the hon. member about the number of diplomatic communications going back a number of years. The most recent were on November 28, 1980 and December 5, 1980. I could give the hon. member a whole list of what has been done. With the change of administration in the United States, we are now making an effort to discuss the recommendations in the latest 1JC special report.

subtopic: NATIVE RIGHTS-AGREEMENT WITH COMMITTEE FOR ORIGINAL PEOPLES ENTITLEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIVE RIGHTS-AGREEMENT WITH COMMITTEE FOR ORIGINAL PEOPLES ENTITLEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 2, I raised with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the question of the government's failure to honour agreements made with native peoples in Canada. I wish to pursue this question with special reference to the James Bay Agreement which was signed by the Hon. Judd Buchanan for the Government of Canada on November 11, 1975. Section 14 of the agreement provides for the establishment of a Cree regional board of health services and social services. Subsection 22 reads as follows:
The budget from Quebec to the Cree Regional Board shall include funding for the support of health services, which are not included in provincial programs for the general population, but which are provided to the native people by the Department of National Health and Welfare or other agencies.
Section 28.11 of the agreement provides that Quebec and Canada shall provide funding and technical assistance for essential sanitation services in each Cree community.
The government has seen the agreement as an easy way to wash its hands of all responsibility for the native people in the James Bay area. Last summer, at least ten children died of stomach disease. This reflects the lack of adequate sewage, sanitation and a water supply which was supposedly provided for under Section 28 of the agreement. The governments of Quebec and of Canada must take responsibility for this epi-
Adjournment Debate
demic and for those deaths, because of their slowness in establishing proper sanitary facilities.
But even after these deaths, even after this epidemic had come to public attention, what happened? Because of disagreements over financing the Quebec government put the Cree board under trusteeship. Cree communities were without services from local clinics and hospitals because there was no funding available to pay health staff. This trusteeship was lifted last week, but the problem continues. The Cree have stepped into the crisis by spending other moneys to take emergency correctional moves.
Last September, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) promised that there would be $1 million to help cover these emergency measures. However, like so many of the promises of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, when the time came to work out the details these people were told that there was no money available. They were told that the money would have to be found in their housing budget. It is estimated that a permanent solution to the problems of health and sewage in these communities will cost at least $10-million in capital funds. The government offered only $3 million and said that the other funds will have to come from the general revenues of the Cree. This is a complete denial of the requirements of the agreement.
Last week, in a letter from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), she said:
I am following the situation very closely. However, 1 have been advised that to take any action beyond what I have described, unless it was at the request of the Cree board of health and social services and the ministry of social affairs of Quebec, would put the federal government in breach of the James Bay agreement.
The Cree board of health and social services has requested help. They have requested that the federal government step in and provide some assistance. It is shameful for the government to say that it is helpless to do anything; it is shameful for it to hide behind the James Bay agreement and say that nothing more can be done.
The credibility of the government is on the line. We have talked about the recognition of aboriginal rights in the Constitution, but there is a very clear indication that words are one thing and deeds are another. The COPE agreement is in difficulty because the minister wants the people of that area to make compromises. After an agreement in principle was signed by the government, the people are being asked to make compromises. The government is not living up to the requirements of the James Bay agreement.
What is the government doing? What long-term measures is it taking to ensure that the health of the James Bay Cree communities will be protected? What measures is it taking to ensure that Quebec lives up to its part of the agreement? What is it doing to ensure that its word, given on behalf of the Canadian people, will be honoured?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Chenier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NATIVE RIGHTS-AGREEMENT WITH COMMITTEE FOR ORIGINAL PEOPLES ENTITLEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his very important question, but we

February 23, 1981
Adjournment Debate
must realize that at this point the Grand Council of the Cree are alleging that both Canada and Quebec have failed to fulfil their obligations regarding health services, and that it is bringing the two governments to court.
The federal government has been committed and remains committed to the agreement. To say that nothing has been done is not absolutely correct, since on September 19 there was a meeting with Chief Diamond. At that time, short-term sanitation repairs to Rupert House and Nemiscau were discussed and an amount of $941,000 was allocated to it.
The discussions continued for the months of September, October and November when the details were being hammered out. But when the Quebec government took over the trusteeship of their health services and the Cree made a request that this be removed, it brought the whole case to court. At that point, we backed off. We are still waiting to
testify in those hearings, but we have not been requested to do so yet. The suit against Canada has not been heard, nor has a schedule been hammered out.
As the hon. member indicated, the trusteeship has been removed. There seem to be indications of a rapprochement between Chief Diamond and the Quebec government. This may bring about a solution.
It is very important to repeat that the allegations about Canada not remaining committed are not true. We are fulfilling our responsibilities and we intend to continue fulfilling them. The minister remains willing to do whatever he can to resolve the matter without resorting to further legal action.
